Climate/Terrain: Tropical and sub-tropical forest; Organization: Tribal; Active Times: Day; Diet: Omnivore; Reaction Modifier: +2; THAC0: 16; Morale: Steady (13)

Beastmen are primitive humanoids of the jungle who live by hunting and gathering.

Appearance: Beastmen are a little shorter (about 5 feet) and slimmer than most humans, covered from head to foot in a soft green pelt over a shorter black undercoat. By tensing and relaxing muscles under the skin they can make the green fur ripple to show the black beneath, so that when they wish (when hunting, say) they blend into the forest in moving patterns of green and black like the shadows of leaves. This makes them almost invisible in woodland: they surprise opponents on 1-4 and are effectively 90% concealed at more than 30 feet in wooded areas. They are well suited to life in the trees, with long toes that help in climbing, though not long enough to hang by. Apart from the fur, their faces look very human. They seldom wear clothing or ornaments of any kind.

Combat: Beastmen are not aggressive and attack only when threatened, but their camouflage and magic resistance make them formidable when forced to fight. They usually carry primitive spears, stone axes, blowguns and bolas, used to great effect from hiding. Blowgun darts are usually tipped with a weak poison (save at +4). They also drop large weighted nets woven from creepers onto enemies from above, to take them alive. If the tribe judges it safe, prisoners are disarmed and released, though some distance from the village and sometimes in dangerous country. Prisoners judged a threat even unarmed are killed painlessly.

Most encounters are with hunting parties gathering food for the tribe. If the beastmen gain surprise, they usually follow the intruders, attacking only if they think they must.

Habitat/Society: By many measures beastmen seem primitive, and their common name strengthens that view, but the beastmen of the Amedio Jungle are far from stupid, and other races could learn from how they organize themselves. A tribe has up to 60 members. Its central figure is the "chief," though the word misleads: the chief does not seek the post and is not elected or chosen. When a decision must be made or the tribe led, someone leads, always the one best suited to the task at hand and always with the tribe's support, and who that is may change from day to day as circumstances change.

This is not random: if someone tries to lead without the tribe's support, he or she is simply ignored. The loose arrangement works because every member of the tribe takes part in every decision. For outsiders, though, it makes talking and negotiating with a tribe difficult; the answer to "take me to your leader" depends on the situation.

Males and females are completely equal. The only time a female does not share in every part of tribal life is when she is pregnant and very near to giving birth. The whole tribe raises the young; about 10% of a tribe are immature (10-80% grown). The young show camouflage ability from birth but do not hunt or gather until they mature at 10 years. Beastmen live about 50 years. The tribe cares for its elderly as it does for children; they are usually about 5% of a tribe.

Tribes live in the trees, in shelters cleverly woven from living branches. Each holds one family: 3-4 adults of both sexes in a loose group marriage, with their children.

Unlike most other "primitive" peoples, beastmen have no religion at all. They do not believe in gods, spirits, ghosts, magic or anything supernatural; if they cannot touch and measure it, it does not exist. So they have no shamans or witch doctors. Whether this belief comes from their resistance to magic, or somehow causes it, is unknown.

Beastmen keep to themselves and deal only with other beastman tribes. They make and use few objects and so care little for trade. They have their own language, and a few can speak the common tongue haltingly. Most of them seem to live in the Amedio Jungle, though tribes are said to live in the jungles of Hepmonaland too.

Niche: Beastmen are at the top of the food chain. They hunt smaller forest animals and gather edible plants, with no interest in farming or herding. Large jungle carnivores hunt them, often without much success thanks to the beastmen's intelligence. They make very little beyond weapons and simple tools and care almost nothing for luxuries. Their way of life supports itself and depends on no trade, though they might consider trading in special circumstances.

Climate/Terrain: All desert; Organization: Solitary; Active Times: Any; Diet: Special; Reaction Modifier: −3; THAC0: 16; Morale: Fanatical (20)

Vampire cacti are plants of the deep desert that add to their water supply by draining the fluids of animals that come within reach.

Appearance: A vampire cactus looks like a century plant, with 12 fleshy leaves, each tipped with a sharp needle about an inch long. From its central core rises a single spike 5-6 feet tall. The leaves are about 5 feet long but droop toward the ground, so the main body of the plant stands about 3 feet high. They are dusty green with a narrow yellow edge; the needles are white and the spike golden yellow. Each midsummer a single small blood-red flower opens at the tip of the spike, and once pollinated it forms a small blood-red fruit, moist and sweet and almost irresistible to most birds.

The plant is rooted in place but can move its leaves quickly. It is usually surrounded by the skeletons and drained bodies of warm-blooded desert creatures such as kangaroo rats.

Combat: The cactus attacks by shooting the needles on its leaf tips into a victim. They have a range of 3 yards and stay attached to the leaves by a thick, rubbery thread that unreels from inside the leaf; the plant drains its victim's fluids through this thread.

  • Each needle does 1-2 points of damage when it strikes. Each round after, the plant drains 1-3 points of fluid (that is, blood) through every needle still in the victim's flesh.
  • The victim can tear free or pull the needles out, but they are cruelly barbed: pulling one out does 1-3 points of damage.
  • The plant can fire all twelve needles at once, but no more than six at one target, and can engage as many targets as it has needles.
  • A needle that misses is reeled in and ready to fire again in 30 seconds. When a target dies, the plant reels in those needles and readies them for the next victim.
  • After draining 50 points of damage the plant is sated. It reels in all its needles and attacks nothing for 48 hours.

The threads are very tough: AC 8, taking 4 hp to cut. The leaves are AC 7 and each takes 1+1 hit dice of damage. Damage to threads or leaves does the plant no lasting harm, since it regrows a damaged leaf in 5-8 days, though destroying a leaf or cutting a thread reduces its number of attacks. The only way to kill it is to destroy the core, which is AC 6 and takes 3 hit dice of damage; damage to the leaves does not count against this. Because the moving leaves surround the core, any attack aimed at the core has a 75% chance of hitting a leaf instead.

Vampire cacti are immune to lightning and electrical attacks, which they ground into the desert through their roots, but fire does double damage to them. Having no mind, they are unaffected by sleep, charm, illusions and other mind-affecting magic.

Habitat/Society: These plants of the Bright Desert developed their blood-draining to meet their need for water. Other adaptations to the deep desert are the dusty surface of their leaves (to slow evaporation), the single small flower (to lose little water) and roots that carry electricity, since they are often the tallest things around and are frequently struck by desert lightning. Migrating birds seem to have carried their seeds to the edges of the Dry Steppes and even to the forbidding Sea of Dust, where some are found.

The only treasure near a vampire cactus is whatever its unlucky victims carried.

Niche: Nothing eats the vampire cactus; its flesh is too tough and bitter, unlike its fruit. Anything warm-blooded is a possible victim.

Climate/Terrain: Temperate barrens and hills; Organization: Pack; Active Times: Night; Diet: Omnivore; Reaction Modifier: +1; THAC0: 17; Morale: Shaky (6)

Camprats are small rodents with appetites far bigger than they are. They are generally harmless, but their knack for getting their teeth into anything edible drives travelers to distraction. They have many other names across the continent, most of them unprintable.

Appearance: Camprats look like prairie dogs or small gophers. Their fur is light sandy brown, darkening to dark brown or even black in a streak down the spine, and they have a tiny stub of a tail, small beady eyes, and long, very sharp front teeth. They move very fast and can climb almost anything.

Combat: Camprats are timid and fight only when cornered, but then their razor-sharp front teeth go through leather as easily as thin cloth. They would much rather flee, climbing, jumping over or gnawing through whatever is in the way. Unlike ordinary rats they are clean and carry no real risk of disease. They are so quick that they are hard to hit, hence their fairly good armor class.

Habitat/Society: Like rats, camprats live in loose packs with about equal numbers of males and females, with no leader and hardly any organization. A female mates once every nine months, bearing litters of 6-8, of which about two-thirds usually survive. While she bears and raises her young, about 3 months, she stays in her lair (usually a small cave, a gap between rocks, or a hole she has dug), and the male brings food for her and the young. When the young are grown and leave, the pair part.

Camprats can make astonishing leaps, up to eight feet across and three feet up, and can climb any surface that gives their tiny claws the slightest hold. Their front teeth grow all the time, so they must gnaw to keep them short, which also keeps them sharp. A camprat chews through thick cloth (a sack, say) in five seconds, thin leather in 15 seconds and thick leather in 30 seconds. Even wood is little obstacle: an inch takes 60 seconds (soft wood) to 90 seconds (hard wood).

Their diet is simple: if it is not on fire, they eat it. They scavenge constantly and go to great lengths to steal food. The usual precautions, such as storing food overnight in thick leather sacks or hanging it from branches, do not stop them, making them a great nuisance to travelers in barrens and hills.

Experienced travelers take dead trees as a warning that camprats are about: the creatures gnaw the bark, often enough to ring the trunk and kill the tree. Camprats are annoyingly common in most hills and barrens, including the Hestmark Highlands, the Abbor-Alz and the Kron Hills. Tales say a gnome king centuries ago spent ten years trying to rid the Kron Hills of camprats, without success, of course.

Niche: Camprats are pure scavengers that eat anything they find but do not hunt. They have good reason to be timid: many large carnivores think them delicacies. Ogres love live camprats, and red dragons often breathe fire into camprat holes and then dig out the cooked snacks.

Climate/Terrain: Temperate forest, grassland and forested hills; Organization: Solitary; Active Times: Any; Diet: Carnivore; Reaction Modifier: +1; THAC0: 15; Morale: Elite (17)

Changecats are felines with two forms: one exactly like an ordinary house cat, the other like a large plains cat such as a cheetah. A changecat can shift between them at will. In the statistics, figures outside parentheses are for the house cat form and figures inside parentheses for the plains cat form.

Appearance: In its small form a changecat cannot be told from a house cat, and its coloring ranges from pure black through tabby to pure white, as house cats' does. Only its eyes differ: they are even steadier than a normal cat's, and more confident. In its large form it has the size and lines of a cheetah, sleek, powerful and very fast, but its coat is tawny like a lion's, without the cheetah's spots. Like a cheetah's, its claws do not retract, serving for grip as well as fighting.

Combat: As a house cat, the changecat has one effective attack with its front claws; if it hits, it may also rake with its rear claws (treat as one attack). As a plains cat it has two front claw attacks, and if both hit it may rake with both rear claws (treat as separate attacks). In either form it moves so silently that it surprises prey on 1-3 in 6, and its keen senses and instincts mean it is surprised only on 1 in 6. Its balance and agility are such that it always lands on its feet.

Changing form takes one round, and a changecat can change up to five times a day, with no limit on how long it stays in either form. It usually spends most of its time as a house cat but turns into a plains cat at once if threatened, becoming a dangerous foe.

As a house cat it seldom attacks anything bigger than itself, preferring mice, small rats and birds. As a plains cat it hunts larger prey such as deer or antelope, stalking to within 100 yards or so and then bursting from cover to run the prey down at its amazing sprinting speed. It can sprint for two rounds and must then rest two rounds before sprinting again.

Habitat/Society: The changecat is the result of a Rel Astran wizard's experiments many decades ago. Trying to create the perfect animal companion and guardian, he magically altered an ordinary house cat's DNA (the book's word) and produced the first changecat. To his surprise the trait bred true: changecats can breed with any feline, and all the young have the full abilities of a changecat.

Though they arose east of the Grandwood Forest, changecats have spread steadily west and across the world. They are solitary, at least toward other felines, and breed only once a year, with small litters of one to three; luckily so, or they might overrun the world. A changecat must eat enough to support its body in whatever form it holds, so it pays to stay a house cat as much as possible: a small cat can easily find enough food where a cheetah might struggle.

Changecats are drawn to humans, elves and half-elves. They are suspicious of the smaller demi-humans (halflings, gnomes and dwarves) and strongly dislike half-orcs. A changecat treated kindly by a human or demi-human is likely (75%) to adopt that person and travel along. Once it has adopted a companion it normally stays a house cat, giving no hint that it is more than it seems. If its companion is threatened, there is a 50% chance it changes form and fights in defense. It never hunts humans or demi-humans, or attacks them unprovoked.

Niche: The changecat is at the top of the food chain. It seldom hunts intelligent creatures, preferring herd animals as easier prey. As a plains cat it has no natural enemies (except perhaps humans). As a house cat it may be hunted by larger creatures that would normally eat cats, but they are in for a nasty and possibly fatal surprise.

Climate/Terrain: Temperate and sub-tropical mountains; Organization: Swarm; Active Times: Night; Diet: Nil; Reaction Modifier: −5; THAC0: Nil (13); Morale: See below

The crystalmist is a swarm of living crystals found high in the mountains. When threatened, the members of the swarm can join into communities with greater intelligence and powers. In the statistics, figures before parentheses are for a single creature and figures inside parentheses for a community.

Appearance: A single crystalmist looks like a tiny drifting crystal, like a large snowflake glowing from within with light of any color. They gather in large, many-colored swarms that drift aimlessly through the air. When the swarm is threatened, the crystals merge into larger communities about a foot across, each made of 50 individuals and taking one round to form. Communities can hover and move slowly, and glow with pure white light.

Combat: Individuals cannot fight and have no measurable intelligence. Communities have animal awareness and can fire brilliant beams of white light with a range of 20 feet, strong enough to do damage and to set alight flammable materials that fail a saving throw against magical fire. Armor can absorb or reflect the beams (sometimes at the cost of catching fire), so the beams use a normal hit roll rather than a spell attack and saving throw. If a community misses but still rolls more than 3 (what it needs to hit AC 10), the beam has struck the target's shield or a piece of armor. If that item is flammable (padded armor, a wooden shield and so on), it must save against magical fire or burst into flame.

A community of 50 individuals has 50 hp, but if it takes 10 or more points of damage it breaks apart into its individuals. Each point of damage destroys one individual, so a community that takes 12 points falls apart at once into 38 individuals. Crystals from a broken community cannot form a new one for 5 rounds.

Crystalmists, single or in communities, are immune to sleep, charm, illusions and other mind-affecting magic. Their awareness is limited and brief, so they have no morale in the usual sense: within the limits above, they keep forming communities and attacking until the threat to the swarm is gone or they are all destroyed.

Habitat/Society: A single crystalmist is less aware and intelligent than an insect, but over thousands of years they have developed the ability to merge into larger communities when needed, joining their tiny minds into an animal-level intelligence. Communities form whenever a creature tries to pass through a swarm; most mountain creatures know this and avoid the drifting lights.

By day crystalmists lie inert on the ground like scattered salt crystals, without glow or movement. During daylight they absorb what little they need from the air and rocks (oxygen, hydrogen, silicon, some carbon and other trace elements) along with the energy of sunlight, which they somehow store in their crystal structure for later use. They reproduce rarely, by splitting in two like single-celled creatures.

They may be found in any temperate or subtropical mountain range but are most common in the Crystalmist Mountains; sages still argue over whether the range was named for the creatures or the creatures for the range.

Niche: Since they consume nothing but energy and lifeless matter, crystalmists are at the bottom of the food chain. Some night hunters, mostly birds and bats, get needed minerals from them, snatching a few from the air before communities can form to drive them off. Slow-moving and earthbound creatures tend to avoid them.

Climate/Terrain: Temperate cities; rarely, temperate hills, barrens or forested hills; Organization: Solitary; Active Times: Any; Diet: Omnivore; Reaction Modifier: +2; THAC0: 10; Morale: Fanatical (20)

Greyhawk dragons love the company of humankind and prefer to live in cities. They are highly magical and scholarly.

Appearance: Though much smaller than many of its kin, the Greyhawk dragon has the strength and toughness typical of dragons. Its scales are a rich metallic grey like brushed steel, darkening to almost the blue-black of gunmetal on its underside and toward its tail. Its wing membranes have the sheen of fine silk.

Combat: At heart a peaceful creature, the Greyhawk dragon avoids fighting where it can, but when combat cannot be avoided it fights with great intelligence and deadliness. Besides its claw/claw/bite attacks, three times a day it can breathe out a highly poisonous gas (save vs. poison at -4 or die). At most it can breathe enough to fill a cube 30 feet on a side, but it can measure out smaller amounts carefully. The gas is quickly absorbed through the skin and is just as deadly that way as breathed. Coating all bare skin with lard or other grease gives partial protection (the save is then at -2). The poison does not last: within two minutes of contact with air the gas becomes harmless.

The dragon would rather use magic than physical attacks. At the very young age it has four 1st level spells, and at each later age bracket it gains four spells of the next higher level (so at old age it has four spells of each level from 1st to 6th). From birth it can also polymorph self five times a day, with unlimited duration, unlike the magic-user spell.

It is immune to magic-user spells of 1st-4th level and has 75% magic resistance against all other magic. It can use any magic item allowed to magic-users.

Habitat/Society: Out of love for and fascination with humanity, a Greyhawk dragon usually lives polymorphed into human form, preferably in a large city, where it typically owns a large house and is often the center of artistic and scholarly gatherings: poetry readings, discussion groups and the like. In their human guises these dragons are often well known among scholars and patrons of the arts. They keep their true nature absolutely secret.

Food is usually its biggest problem: it may look like a man or woman, but it must eat enough to keep up its true bulk. Every two weeks or so it disappears to nearby wild country, where it may claim to own a hunting lodge, and hunts to make up for its (by dragon standards) enforced fast in the city. Like other dragons it eats anything but prefers fresh meat. It never takes domestic herds, hunting wild animals instead, especially those dangerous to people.

Greyhawk dragons are very rare; even the largest city may have only one or two living secretly within it. Though they take great care to hide their nature, one Greyhawk dragon recognizes another on sight. Dragons in the same city are usually friendly but do not normally seek each other out. Every twelve years a Greyhawk dragon looks for a mate, often from another city. The pair retire to the wilderness to raise a single young one, and once it can fend for itself, at about 24 months, the parents part and return to their own lives. They very rarely choose the same mate twice.

They speak their own language and those of most humans, demi-humans and humanoids, and can be found, if they wish to be, in any large town or city. There are said to be no fewer than five in the city whose name they bear, though nobody, least of all the dragons, seems willing or able to prove it.

Niche: Greyhawk dragons are at the top of the food chain, with no natural enemies. In cities they seldom work as craftsmen, preferring to gather and spread knowledge, as sages do.

Climate/Terrain: Tropical and sub-tropical swamp; Organization: Tribal; Active Times: Day; Diet: Carnivore; Reaction Modifier: +1; THAC0: 18; Morale: Steady (13)

Grung are fiercely territorial, toadlike humanoids of swamps and marshes. They look much like frogs and other amphibians, and may in fact be descended from them.

Appearance: Grung stand about 3 feet tall. The lower body is much like a giant frog's or toad's, with powerful legs and large webbed feet, but the upper body is more developed, with muscular arms, opposable thumbs and a smaller, more humanlike head. They stand upright and move in quick, short hops, but cannot make the huge leaps of frogs, toads or bullywugs. Their evolution gave them intelligence and hands for tools but took away the frog's grasping tongue; instead their wide mouths are full of sharp meat-eater's teeth.

Like other amphibians they have slick skin, and since they breathe through it, they must keep it moist. They are colored like bullfrogs, mottled green and brown on the back and white or yellow on the belly. Their eyes, smaller than their ancestors' and guarded by bony ridges, are red with black pupils. Males are a little smaller than females, but both are equally aggressive and dangerous.

Combat: Being small, grung prefer ambush to open attack. Their favorite tactic is to lie hidden until their enemies, whether travelers or grung of another tribe, walk into the killing ground, and then open fire with short bows and spears. Against anyone but grung these attacks are especially deadly, because grung always poison their arrowheads and spear points with a poison their own skin produces: before using a weapon, a grung wipes it on its skin. The poison is deadly to non-grung (save vs. poison or die unpleasantly in 1-4 minutes); grung are immune. It breaks down quickly in air and is harmless after 10 minutes. A dead grung's skin also stops being poisonous 10 minutes after death.

Grung prefer bow and spear but can give a nasty bite. Their saliva is also poisonous, though much weaker than their skin (save at +2).

A grung dies if its skin dries out: it must immerse itself in water for at least a minute every three hours, or suffocate, because dry skin cannot take in enough air. The water around a grung settlement is tainted by their poison; any non-grung who drinks it must save vs. poison at +3 or be nauseated for 2-8 rounds (attacking and defending at -1).

Habitat/Society: Grung are warlike and extremely territorial, usually claiming everything within a mile of their village. Anyone foolish enough to enter is attacked at once. Grung of other tribes are fair game too, and nasty little border wars between neighbors are normal. Most encounters are with roaming war bands.

A village is an untidy cluster of crude shelters, sometimes hidden inside large dead trees. A tribe has up to 100 members, 25% of them young. Like the frogs they came from, grung lay eggs, and the young pass through a tadpole stage (AC 10; MV //12"; HD ½; #AT 1; Dmg 1; AL LE). Over 3 months the tadpoles absorb their tails and grow limbs, then climb out of the water and join the tribe as young grung of 1-1 HD, able to move and fight from the moment they leave the water. They are fully grown 6 months later.

Grung tribes are ruled by females. All war chiefs are female, and the tribe's chieftain is the strongest fighter among them. A lower-ranking female may challenge the chieftain for her place at any time, always to the death. Each tribe also has one female shaman of up to 3rd level. War chiefs, shamans and the chieftain wear ornaments made from the bones of enemies. Males are kept down and have no voice in any decision.

Grung sometimes take prisoners alive, especially other grung. The prisoners and the bodies of enemies are the main course at tribal feasts.

Grung have their own language and can communicate crudely with frogs, toads and other swamp amphibians. They have no interest in learning the common tongue or other demi-human and humanoid languages: other creatures are for eating, not for talking to.

Niche: When not eating careless travelers (or each other), grung hunt rats and other swamp mammals. Few predators eat them, since their poisonous skin makes a deadly meal, but certain giant snakes are immune and are their greatest danger. Grung are among the deadliest creatures a traveler can meet in the Vast Swamp.

Climate/Terrain: Temperate wilderness forest; Organization: Solitary; Active Times: Night; Diet: Carnivore; Reaction Modifier: −2; THAC0: 16; Morale: Regular (10)

The ingundi is an intelligent humanoid reptile.

Appearance: In its true form the ingundi looks like a small lizard man: a lightly built reptile 5-6 feet tall, walking on two legs, with a tail to balance its upper body. Its mouth is wider than a lizard man's and full of sharp, tearing teeth, and its arms, though thinner and weaker, end in long, hideously sharp claws. It is light green on the back, shading to pale yellowish white on the belly, with small yellow eyes and large black pupils. It wears no clothing or ornament of any kind.

It seldom shows its true form. It has a strong change self power and usually appears as some other, harmless-seeming creature. When hunting humans or demi-humans, it appears as an attractive member of the victim's race, of the opposite sex.

Combat: The ingundi uses its natural powers to choose a victim and lure it away from its herd or group, so that it can kill and eat it at leisure. It has a powerful form of ESP, with which it plucks from the victim's mind the image of the person the victim most wants to meet romantically. Then it takes on that person's appearance with its change self power. It can take the form of any creature from the size of a large dog to that of a bear. It can use this power twice a day, and the effect lasts 1d10+10 rounds unless dispelled sooner. (The book calls the creature "incubus" in this sentence.)

In this form the ingundi approaches its victim and tries to start a conversation (or a courtship ritual, for prey that does not speak), which gives it closer contact with the victim's deepest desires. Playing on them, it casts a strong charm person (or charm monster, as fits) on the victim, who saves at -2 because the creature can reach the depths of the victim's mind.

If the charm works, the ingundi tries to lead the victim away from companions to a place where it can kill and eat in private, and coaxes the victim to take off any armor. Its first attack is at +4 to hit and the victim does not attack that round. After that the charm is broken and the victim can fight back normally.

Spells that guard the mind, such as mind blank, block the ingundi's ESP, and it cannot charm someone so protected. It will not approach anyone whose thoughts it cannot read; if such a shield goes up after it has begun its approach, it withdraws as fast as it can without revealing what it is.

Anyone else watching hears only half a conversation: the victim talks, but the other figure is silent, because the ingundi is not really speaking but creating the conversation inside the victim's mind. Onlookers are immune to its charm; only the chosen target can fall under it. If the charm fails, or someone interferes, the ingundi tries to flee, fighting only if cornered.

Habitat/Society: The ingundi lives alone, usually in a dead tree or among the roots of a living one. Two willingly approach each other only to mate, once a year in the depths of winter. The female lays a single egg in a hidden, sheltered spot and then ignores it completely. It hatches after 12 weeks. The young ingundi is barely two feet long from nose to tail but can fend for itself from birth, with full ESP, change self and charm powers, though it can use them only on small animals. It grows quickly, reaching full size in six months.

Its powers work well on humans and demi-humans, but they are not its usual prey. Normally it reads the minds of other forest creatures, such as deer, and uses change self to look like a harmless member of the victim's species: a doe to catch a stag, a fawn to catch a doe. In that form it comes close and touches the victim, casting its charm with the touch; normal (non-monstrous) animals get no saving throw. It then leads the victim off to kill and eat at leisure.

The ingundi has few natural enemies. Some creatures would eat it if they knew what it was, but it can use its ESP and change self to defend itself too: unless surprised, it senses the thoughts of anything hunting it and takes the form of something the hunter would not eat. It has no language; ingundi communicate by reading each other's thoughts.

Niche: The ingundi is at or near the top of the food chain, an efficient predator of creatures from deer to traveling humans and demi-humans. It produces nothing. Some sages believe ingundi (printed "incubus") are partly to blame for the dark reputations of the Fellreev Forest and the Hornwood.

Climate/Terrain: All mountains; Organization: Solitary; Active Times: Any; Diet: Nil; Reaction Modifier: +5; THAC0: 12; Morale: Steady (14)

The nimbus comes from the Quasi-elemental Plane of Lightning. It visits the Prime Material Plane now and then, but is seen only in high mountain ranges and only in the stormy season (usually Sunsebb through Coldeven).

Appearance: A nimbus is made entirely of electrical energy and has no fixed shape. It usually takes one of four forms: ball lightning (a slowly drifting ball of light easily mistaken for a will o' wisp); sheet lightning (a veil of light like a small aurora); bolt lightning (bolts of light jumping from object to object); or St. Elmo's fire (a soft, flickering glow surrounding an object). It can change form at will. It reaches its top speed of 48" only as bolt lightning; in other forms it moves at most 18". In every form it gives off brilliant white or blue-white light.

Combat: On the Material Plane the nimbus is not aggressive and plays among the mountain peaks for pure joy, but it can defend itself well. Its favorite attack is to wrap its victim in its St. Elmo's fire form and electrocute it; a successful hit means it has engulfed the target and discharged its current. If the target wears armor of iron or steel (not mithral or adamantite) or carries more than 250 gp weight of iron or steel gear, the nimbus gets +2 to hit. It can use this attack only four times a day, since more would drain too much of its energy.

It can also cast small lightning bolts, one a round, to a range of 60 feet, each doing 2-12 points of damage (save for half).

Only +1 or better magic weapons harm a nimbus. Someone who hits it with a weapon of iron or steel takes 1-4 points of electrical damage per hit and has a 25% chance of dropping the weapon. Lightning and electrical attacks do it no harm; each one that strikes it actually restores 3-12 points of damage. Poison and acid have no effect. Fire and cold do normal damage, and magical attacks involving water (such as ice storm) do double damage, though ordinary water does not hurt it. It is immune to sleep, charm, illusions and other mind-affecting magic.

When roused, a nimbus builds up a static charge strong enough to give creatures within 30 feet the uncomfortable feeling of their hair standing on end. Within 10 feet, iron and steel objects glow with their own St. Elmo's fire. This charge does no damage, though it may look dangerous.

Habitat/Society: The nimbus is often wrongly called a "lightning elemental," but it is not a true elemental, only a native of that quasi-elemental plane (as the xorn is of the Elemental Plane of Earth). It reaches the Prime Material Plane through gates that sometimes open at the heart of great thunderstorms, and only storms in high mountains bring it, perhaps because the thin air suits it. For some reason it is especially fond of the Sulhaut Mountains, perhaps because winds from the Sea of Dust carry a static charge of their own that causes terrible lightning storms among those peaks.

On this plane they are solitary; on their own plane they are common and gather in groups. A nimbus does not realize that "bags of mostly water" such as animals are alive. If it thinks about it at all, it is more likely to believe that energy, such as fire and lightning, is alive. How it communicates is unknown; telepathy, tongues and other magic are no use at all for talking with it.

Niche: On the Prime Material Plane the nimbus consumes nothing, produces nothing and has no predators. It draws the energy it needs from the Quasi-elemental Plane of Lightning.

Climate/Terrain: Tropical oceans; Organization: Family; Active Times: Any; Diet: Omnivore; Reaction Modifier: +4; THAC0: 17; Morale: Steady (14)

Sea sprites are shy creatures, much like their cousins on land. They are relentless enemies of anything that would destroy the delicate life of their coral reefs.

Appearance: Sea sprites look like tiny people no more than two feet tall. They have no wings but have delicate webbing between their fingers and toes. Their skin is fine and pale, sometimes slightly bluish, and their hair, usually worn long, is bright green. They usually wear jerkins of eel skin or other soft, supple material, preferring bright sea colors (blues, greens and aquamarines), and often wear finely made ornaments of precious metal. Females are a little smaller and more slender than males.

They carry tiny but wickedly sharp swords, and each has a 50% chance of carrying a light crossbow that works fully under water as well as above. These weapons are far too small for humans or demi-humans, even halflings, to use. Sea sprites can become invisible at will (opponents strike at -4) and can detect good and evil up to 50 yards away.

Combat: Sea sprites avoid face-to-face fighting unless there is no other choice, preferring to attack from ambush with their crossbows. The bolts are tipped with a potion: any creature struck must save vs. poison or fall into a deep sleep for 1-6 hours, which can be deadly for creatures that must surface to breathe. Sea sprites usually kill evil creatures and carry neutral or good ones far from where they were met; air-breathers are usually left above water, on a nearby deserted shore, for instance. The sprites do not usually care what happens to the sleepers afterward.

They often use other sea creatures as pack animals and guards; a group has a 45% chance of having 1-6 meat-eating fish such as barracuda or quippers with it. A sea sprite can grant 2-5 turns of water breathing by touch, can cast airy water once a day at 10th level, and slow (by touch) three times a day at 5th level.

Habitat/Society: Sea sprites live among the coral reefs and warm shallows of the Densac Gulf, the Tilva Strait and the waters to the south. They breathe equally well in water and air but much prefer life under the sea and seldom go ashore. They are joyful creatures who love to play among the brilliant fish of their home waters, darting through the water so fast that they can catch and stroke the quickest reef fish.

They hunt fish with their crossbows but kill only to eat, choose their prey carefully, and tend the fish so that they never run short. They respect, and are respected by, fishermen who take only enough to feed their people; that is the way of the sea. They dislike those who kill too many fish or fish for sport, and they are bitter enemies of anyone who spoils the coral seas, and likely to act against them.

They live in family groups in natural coral caves or in the hulks of ships wrecked on the reefs. The oldest male leads, but the senior female advises him and is often the real power. They believe that wealth the sea has taken, as sunken treasure, should stay with the sea, so they oppose treasure hunters and salvagers of wrecks.

Sea sprites have their own language, and 50% of them speak the common tongue. They can also communicate in a simple way with the more intelligent creatures of the deep. They believe in a balance of nature and so bear no ill will toward sharks and other predators, hating only the evil and cruel sea dwellers, especially sahuagin and their kind, whom they attack on sight.

Niche: Sea sprites are at the top of the reef food chain. Their only natural enemies are sahuagin, and their speed and accurate crossbows make them hard prey. They are friendly with aquatic elves and sometimes trade with them, though the two races never live together.

Swordwraiths are the spirits of warriors cut down in the thick of battle and held back from the dissolution of death by their own unbending will.

Appearance: Seen only at night or underground where the sun never reaches, swordwraiths look like warriors in armor carrying various weapons of war. The armor and weapons are ordinary, but the flesh inside seems insubstantial; in some lights all that shows is two glowing eyes in the shadow of the helmet. They reek of mold and decay, though the smell comes from their armor and weapons, not from the creatures. An aura of intense cold surrounds them, uncomfortable but not damaging.

Combat: In life swordwraiths were hardened warriors, and as undead they keep their knowledge of strategy and tactics, fighting small-unit actions by the book and knowing exactly when to attack, give ground and counterattack. They are intelligent and speak the common tongue of humankind, so they might agree to a parley, but only if it is asked by someone they consider their military equal.

They attack like ordinary warriors with their various weapons, but whatever the weapon, the damage is 1-10 hp, and each hit also drains 1 point of strength. A victim whose strength reaches 0 dies. Strength lost to a swordwraith returns only with complete rest (1 point per day of total inactivity) or through a wish, limited wish or equally powerful magic.

Only +2 or better weapons harm swordwraiths. They are completely immune to sleep, charm and other mind-affecting magic, and are turned as vampires.

Habitat/Society: Swordwraiths were professional soldiers in life, officers, mercenaries and others for whom fighting was everything. Slain on the battlefield, their will was too strong to give up the trade of violent death, and many are so stubborn that they will not admit, even to themselves, that they are dead. They are entirely free-willed and feel no kinship with other undead; in fact they hate the "mindless lack of discipline" of most undead.

They are active only at night or underground away from sunlight. Their bodies were usually buried in barrows or burial mounds, and intruders entering such a barrow by day may find swordwraiths preparing for the night's work.

They gather in small units and councils of war to plan and carry out midnight raids on settlements near the battlefields where they lie, and are likely to attack any traveling party foolish enough to spend the night in their territory. The "lawful" part of their alignment means loyalty within their group, to other swordwraiths and no one else. They take no loot and hold no ground as a result of these raids: they fight because fighting is all they know. If they have a creed, it is "Mercenaries don't die; they just go to Hades to regroup."

Swordwraiths are common in the Stark Mounds, probably because of ancient border wars between Geoff and Sterich or their forerunners, but they may be found anywhere in the world with old battlefields and war graves.

Niche: Swordwraiths consume and produce nothing. Their only victims are travelers who stray into their territory and the people of nearby settlements.

Mist wolves are cousins of ordinary wolves, but larger and with some magical abilities. They are lawful good, but humankind's deep fear and hatred of wolves means they will always be misunderstood.

Appearance: Mist wolves look almost exactly like their non-magical cousins, but stand taller at the shoulder and have smoky grey fur with white tips on the hackles. They are lean and muscular with fearsome teeth. Their eyes are black, without the red tinge often seen in wild wolves.

Combat: Mist wolves hunt in packs like common wolves, often dragging down opponents by sheer numbers. Being more intelligent, they are less likely to keep fighting a battle they are obviously losing. A magical ability helps them break away from stronger foes: twice a day a wolf can breathe out a cloud of thick mist (like a wall of fog spell) that blocks all sight, filling a space 10 feet on a side and lasting five rounds unless blown away. The mist is purely defensive, since the wolves cannot see through it either.

Habitat/Society: Because of their alignment, mist wolves attack humans or demi-humans only when they are behaving in openly evil ways, and normally they protect travelers from evil creatures that would harm them. Unfortunately, fear and hatred of wolves is taught from the cradle and built into everything from children's tales to common sayings ("a wolf in the fold," "the wolf at the door" and the like). It does not help that mist wolves are often seen when evil is about; people never realize, or refuse to believe, that the wolves appear near evil in order to fight it. So mist wolves are often killed by the very people they are trying to protect.

Mist wolves have a natural ability to detect evil that works constantly, without any effort. They are relentless enemies of evil and defenders of good and law, and will go to great lengths, even giving their lives, to protect humans and demi-humans.

Like common wolves, mist wolves live in packs of up to 20, with equal numbers of males and females. The leader is the strongest wolf (usually, but not always, a male), who wins and keeps the position by challenge and non-lethal combat. A pack met in its own territory (usually wild forest) has half as many cubs as females. Mist wolves mate for life and both parents care for the cubs, which grow quickly, gaining their breath weapon at six months and full maturity at 12 months.

They have a rich language of their own made up of yips, barks and growls. They understand the common tongue but cannot speak it because of the shape of their mouths and throats.

Mist wolves are most common in forests with evil reputations, because that is where they can do the most good (which, of course, does nothing for their own reputation). There are large numbers in the Dreadwood and the Burneal Forest, though they are not limited to these places.

Niche: Mist wolves are very efficient predators with few natural enemies. They are intelligent enough to choose their prey and manage their hunting carefully, never overhunting an area or a herd.

Drowned ones, also called sea zombies, are the animated corpses of humans who died at sea. They are like zombies of the land, but they have wills of their own and are said to be animated by the will of Nerull the Reaper.

Appearance: They look just as their name suggests: human corpses that have lain long under water, with bloated, discolored flesh dripping foul water, empty eye sockets and tongues often sticking out between blackened lips. Their looks and stench of decay are so revolting that anyone who sees one or comes within 20 feet must save vs. poison or be nauseated, attacking and defending at -1 for 2-8 rounds. On land they move slowly in a clumsy shuffle, but in water they swim frighteningly fast.

Combat: Like most undead, drowned ones hate the living and attack them whenever they can, often with surprising cunning: luring ships onto rocks, say, and then attacking the sailors as they struggle from the wreck. They use their swimming speed to attack ships at anchor, climbing aboard and trying to drive the sailors overboard, where they are easier to deal with.

They fight with sailors' weapons (short swords, daggers, hooks, clubs and so on), but their unnatural strength means every weapon does 1-10 points of damage. The foul water dripping from them carries disease, so each hit has a 10% chance of giving the victim a severe blood disease.

Their waterlogged flesh takes only half damage from fire and fire magic; lightning, electrical and cold attacks do double damage. They are immune to sleep, charm, illusions and other mind-affecting magic, and because a god's direct will creates them, they cannot be turned like other undead.

Many who become drowned ones were clerics in life and keep their powers. Each drowned one met has a 50% chance of being a cleric of level 1-4 (roll randomly). Nerull grants their spells directly, and they receive only harmful spells.

Habitat/Society: Drowned ones gather in loose packs, driven only by hatred of the living. Being undead they need not eat, though they sometimes tear and chew their victims' flesh, probably just to terrify others.

Under water they are active day and night and are often found in the sunken wrecks of the ships they drowned in. Above water they are active only at night, and they normally stray no more than 100 yards from the water. But when the wind drives a sea fog onto the coast, they can roam inland as far as the fog reaches, returning to the water when the fog retreats or the sun is about to rise. People of foggy coasts usually fear the fog, though they may not know why. In some places, such as the Amedio coast, human sacrifices are often thrown into the fog when it rolls inland, in the hope that the drowned ones will take the offering and leave everyone else alone.

Drowned ones communicate among themselves by a kind of telepathy and need no spoken language except for spellcasting; they speak the verbal parts of spells in hideous, hissing whispers.

They are most common in the shallows of the Azure Sea, perhaps because it supplies a steady stream of raw material in the form of Amedio pirates and freebooters in general. The waters around the Flotsom and Jetsom Islands, Fairwind Isle and the Olman Islands are prime "breeding grounds" for these hideous creatures.

Niche: Drowned ones consume and produce nothing. They work together only to kill more efficiently.

Boccob seldom leaves his own hall. When he does, he appears as a handsome man of no clear age in flowing purple robes covered with shimmering golden runes that move and change. He is indifferent and reserved toward those he meets, neither seeking nor avoiding confrontation, but always looking to gain knowledge.

His most common avatar is hit only by weapons of +3 or better. In any form he can draw power from either the Positive or the Negative Material Plane, letting him strike fear, in a 15 foot radius, into undead or creatures of the Positive or Negative Material Planes (saving throw at -4).

The avatar sees twice as well as normal in every spectrum and regenerates 1d4 hit points per round. Boccob is immune to all spells affecting the mind, including feeblemind and similar magic.

Once a day Boccob can create a disc of Concordant Opposition: a 10-foot web of force that blasts into nothingness any creature with fewer than 10 levels or hit dice, or less than 50% magic resistance, unless it saves. Characters above 10th level take 50 points of damage, no save. Creatures with more than 50% magic resistance are unaffected. Casting time is one segment, and the range is limited only by Boccob's line of sight.

Boccob usually carries his Staff of the Archmage, which combines the powers of a staff of the magi and a wand of conjuration. It can never hold more than 25 charges but can absorb 24 spell levels a day. He always wears at least five amulets and protective devices, including a periapt of wound closure, a scarab of protection, an amulet of proof against detection and location, a periapt of health and a stone of good luck.

Celestian appears as a tall, lean, middle-aged man in black. His symbol, seven "stars" (diamond, amethyst, sapphire, emerald, topaz, jacinth and ruby) blazing with the fire of distant suns, is always part of his dress, worn as an ornament or woven into the cloth. His smooth skin is ebony and his eyes match. He moves quickly and silently and speaks seldom, in a cold, unearthly whisper that carries well despite its softness.

Once per round he can cast any spell involving movement or travel at 18th level, in addition to any spells he has memorized; each casting takes one segment whatever its normal casting time.

He usually carries one or more of these weapons: a long bow +3 with 20 arrows +3; a spear +4, normally 5 feet long but stretching to 10 feet whenever he wishes; a short sword +5; a battle axe +4 he can throw up to 40 feet; and a dagger +6 of unbreakable metal.

Celestian also has the following powers, each usable once a day at will. He (or a cleric casting them) must be under the open sky to use them. Casting is instantaneous, and saves, where allowed, are at -3.

  • Aurora: a motionless hollow cylinder of shimmering light, seven feet high, surrounds Celestian or any creature he chooses within 20 yards. Its radius is anything from one to seven feet, as he chooses, and it lasts up to seven turns unless he dispels it. Celestian and his clerics are unaffected, but any other living thing touching or touched by the light takes 3d8 damage (save vs. spells for half). A creature that fails its save cannot leave the aurora, and anyone trying to enter must also save to get in. The cylinder overcomes magic resistance.
  • Comet: a flaming missile that unerringly strikes one target within 20 yards, setting alight anything flammable it touches. Its poisonous, burning gases do 5d6 damage (save vs. spells for half). The target must stay in sight throughout. Even fire-resistant creatures take full damage; Celestian and his clerics are immune.
  • Heat Lightning: calls a bolt of lightning from the sky that unerringly strikes one target within 70 feet for 5d10 damage (save vs. spells for half). The target must stay in sight throughout. Even creatures resistant to electricity take full damage; Celestian and his clerics are immune.
  • Meteors: 7-16 (1d10+6) stone spheres, each six inches across, fly from Celestian's hand at one target within 20 yards or spread among several. Each does 1d10+4 damage (save vs. spells negates, one save per meteor that strikes). They may be released one at a time or together, but any not released within two turns are lost.
  • Space Chill: a wave of cold and vacuum, 40 feet wide and 70 feet long, pours from Celestian's hands, killing all plants it touches. Other living things take 4d10 damage (save vs. spells for half).
  • Star Shine: a blazing sheet of white light streams from Celestian's eyes, enveloping up to four creatures up to 70 feet away and blinding them for one turn (save vs. spells negates). Cure blindness or a successful dispel magic removes the blindness.
  • Thunder: a great rolling thunderclap sounds directly over Celestian's head. All creatures within 30 feet with fewer than 20 hit dice (except Celestian and his clerics) are stunned for one round and deafened for 1d4+1 rounds, with no save. Creatures from 30 to 70 feet away are only deafened (save vs. spells negates).

St. Cuthbert leaves his plane only when some great duty calls. He hates evil, but cares most for law and order and for the twin tasks of converting the ignorant and keeping the faithful from straying. He usually appears as a stout, ruddy man with apple cheeks, flowing white hair and a drooping moustache, wearing plate mail +5. His helmet is topped with a crumpled hat, and a starburst of rubies set in platinum hangs at his neck. He carries a bronzewood cudgel in his left hand and the Mace of St. Cuthbert in his right.

He has also been known to appear as a yokel covered in manure, a wanderer in brown and green robes, or a slight old tinker. His avatars are hit only by weapons of +2 or better.

The bronzewood cudgel is a +3 weapon that counts as a morning star in his hands. Anyone it touches must save vs. spells or be beguiled for 5-20 turns. The Mace of St. Cuthbert is a mace of disruption +5. On a natural 20, the creature struck permanently loses one point of intelligence, with no save, though a successful magic resistance roll prevents it. The mace also has these powers at 18th level: bless (by touch), know alignment (once a day), tongues and remove curse (seven a week).

Ehlonna appears as a human or elven woman. As a human her hair is chestnut or black; as an elf it is pale gold or coppery gold. In either form her eyes are startling blue or soft violet and her skin clear and fair. Her dress varies from the practical clothes of a forester or ranger to the delicate gown of an elven princess.

In human form she can summon and command horses, and in elven form unicorns, calling them from as far as three miles away. Summoned creatures gladly serve as mounts and do any task she gives them as well as they can. Elves, brownies, gnomes and halflings are especially close to Ehlonna: if she asks a service of any good or neutral member of these races, there is a 90% chance it is granted, whatever it is.

Her most common avatar is struck only by weapons of +1 or better and has the abilities of a 10th level ranger. It always wears iron bracers that give armor class 0 and +2 to all saving throws, and carries a long bow with 40 arrows, a long sword and a dagger. The bow never misses, even at its longest range (21"). Half the arrows are arrows of slaying against various evil woodland animals and creatures; the rest are arrows +3. The long sword is a defender +6 and the dagger is +4.

Fharlanghn appears as an old, weathered man with deeply wrinkled skin and bright, youthful green eyes. He wears plain clothes, usually leather and unbleached linen, always travel-stained but seldom dirty. He seems to move slowly and deliberately but is actually very nimble. He greets fellow travelers politely and is always glad to talk, though never for long.

Fharlanghn speaks every language of Oerth and can communicate with any intelligent creature by telepathy. He can read languages and magic, and at will can detect charm, evil, good, illusion, magic, and snares and pits. He can curse an enemy so that any journey longer than one league takes twice as long as normal, with no save. The curse lasts a month and can be lifted only by a priest of Fharlanghn of 10th level or higher or by a deity able to cast remove curse.

When he has the initiative he can attack and then leap clear of an opponent, as if wearing boots of striding and springing, except that he never falls after a leap. He is never surprised on the Prime Material Plane and is immune to any spell involving earth.

His most common avatar is hit only by weapons of +2 or better, regenerates 1 hit point per melee round, and has the abilities of a 9th level thief. In any form he can cast the following spells, one at a time, once per round, at 18th level: dig, polymorph self, dimension door, pass without trace, dispel magic, plant door, earthquake, rock to mud, find the path, stone tell, improved invisibility, transport via plants, move earth, wall of thorns, pass plant, wind walk, passwall. These are in addition to any spells he has memorized, and each takes one segment to cast.

He always carries the Oerth Disc, an ornate version of his holy symbol: an artifact six inches across, made of many kinds of wood inlaid with jade and turquoise and set with a bright amber gem. By concentrating on it, Fharlanghn can call up a tiny image of any place on the Prime Material Plane. After looking at the image for one round he can teleport there without error, and others who study it for a round can teleport there as if they had studied the place carefully.

Once every ten rounds the Disc can also shoot a burning golden ray at one of three strengths:

  • Pale yellow: as bright as continual light, lighting an area six feet across and up to 600 feet long.
  • Brilliant gold: bright enough to blind any creature permanently (save vs. spells negates). The ray is eight inches across and up to 60 feet long. Creatures struck in the eyes who save, and all creatures within three feet of the ray, are dazzled and blinded for one round.
  • Fiery red: a pencil-thin beam up to 16 feet long that cuts through almost anything: 1/2 inch of stone or 1/4 inch of steel in one blast. Creatures struck take 10-60 (10d6) damage (save vs. spells negates). Its heat instantly sets fire to anything flammable it touches.

Incabulos appears as a hideous man of no clear age, his skin tinged a diseased blue, with a twisted, nightmarish face, a deformed body and skeletal limbs. He wears a filthy dead-black robe lined with sickly orange and trimmed in moss green. He visits the Prime Material Plane only in darkness, riding a nightmare with maximum hit points when he pleases.

Once a day Incabulos can gate in four night hags or eight hordlings (one kind or the other, never a mix). The gate always opens, and one creature arrives each round until all have come. They serve willingly.

His most common avatar is hit only by weapons of +3 or better, regenerates 2 hit points per round, and has the abilities of a 13th level thief. Once a day he can cast a double-strength sleep, taking two segments. Once a day he can also cast a permanent sleep on any creature he touches, from which only an exorcise spell can wake the victim (save vs. spells negates).

His favorite weapon is his staff of wounding, which combines the powers of a staff of withering and a reversed staff of curing. It has 60 charges, and only Incabulos can recharge it.

Istus appears in many guises: sometimes an old crone, sometimes a noble lady, a shepherd girl or a gentlewoman. She always seems unarmed but can make any object an effective weapon doing 1d6 damage. No one knows where she dwells; most likely it is a pocket universe or a demi-plane in the Deep Ethereal that only she and her strands of fate can enter.

Istus is never surprised. Because she can sway fate, she always hits when attacking with an object, though the damage varies, since her control is not that fine. Once a day she can step into the future and back in an instant; each such trip restores 3d10 × 10 lost hit points.

She is immune to all time-related spells (such as augury, divination, time stop and tempus fugit), however they are used. A noble time elemental with maximum hit points always attends her, but goes with her avatar only 20% of the time. Her most common avatar is hit only by weapons of +3 or better.

She always carries the Spindle of Fate, a golden rod wound with silver-grey thread, which answers only to her. While she has it, she can move freely through all times and places. If it is lost, she returns at once to her home and makes a new one, and the lost artifact crumbles to dust. Making a new Spindle takes 3d10 × 10 days, during which she cannot control fate.

With the Spindle, Istus casts strands and webs. Strands have a range of 60 feet and webs 30 feet (except the web of stars, which is always centered on her). She casts them at 24th level. She has often granted strand casting to her high clerics, but never more than two strands a day.

  • Strand of binding (three times a day): the creature struck must save vs. spells or be held motionless, as if bound in heavy iron chains, for 100 rounds minus its hit dice, whatever its strength.
  • Strand of cancellation (twice a day): any non-living object struck is treated as if it had never existed. Only non-living things are affected. Magic items save at 5% per plus or equivalent; artifacts save at 50% and relics at 75%, plus 5% per plus (an artifact sword +4 saves at 70%).
  • Strand of death (once a day): any creature struck, even a deity, is turned to dust; if its magic resistance or save vs. spells fails, it is gone forever.
  • Strand of hostility (twice a day): the creature struck becomes hostile to anyone or anything opposing Istus (save vs. spells negates) and does whatever it must to defend her, even turning on old companions and friends, for fate decrees it. The effect is permanent and only Istus can remove it.
  • Strand of passage (twice a day): instantly links the plane Istus is on with any other plane she wishes. Any creature touching it is carried to the other plane at once. It lasts three rounds and works in one direction only.
  • Strand of sending (at will): the creature struck is sent to the place and future time (up to 200 days ahead) where the DM judges its freedom or life to be in greatest danger (save vs. spells negates; willing creatures need not save). Istus can also use it to send a creature to the time and place of greatest opportunity in the near future.
  • Web of enmeshment (once a day): all creatures caught in this 30-cubic-foot web become lost in a misty maze of unlimited size, where they can see only ten feet. They are filled with nameless dread and have a 50% chance of attacking any creature they meet, friend or foe. The web lasts one turn, but creatures may escape sooner: those not in combat may save vs. spells on the second round and each round after until they escape. A creature with magic resistance rolls when struck; if it succeeds it is not caught, and if it fails it is trapped until it saves. Creatures killed or knocked out in the maze stay there until another creature removes them.
  • Web of entropy (once a day): this invisible, 30-cubic-foot web affects all magical energy within it for one turn. Magic items in it must save as if struck by a strand of cancellation each round, and spells cast from, into or through it are negated.
  • Web of stars (once a day): carries Istus and every creature within 15 feet to a boundless time and space in an unknown place, perhaps her home. It is an extra-dimensional path to anywhere or anywhen, for one who knows the way, and Istus does. Others see an endless starry space filled with silken strands, where distances are warped and one step may cover a vast distance; creatures more than two "steps" away look like glowing stars of red, orange, yellow, green, blue, violet or white. The web lasts one hour, or 600 "steps" of time. Creatures of supra-genius intelligence can find their way back to where they started. Those above supra-genius can find other points along the web (10% chance per point of intelligence over 20) and use it to travel to other planes and times. Creatures of genius intelligence can also grasp the nature of the place (1% chance per point of intelligence) and find points along it, but must study each portal for one turn (100 "steps") before using it. Each creature may try to understand the place only once per visit. Points along the web lie 3d8 steps apart. Creatures still in the web when it fades are instantly teleported to a random place on their home planes.

Nerull appears as a skeletal figure with dull rust-red skin. Locks of ropy dark green hair hang from his skull-like head, and his eyes, talons and teeth are the green of verdigris. He wears a black cowl and carries the Life Cutter, a red-veined staff of sablewood. He appears on the Prime Material Plane only in darkness.

Nerull can fly. All his senses, including infravision and ultravision, are twice as keen as a human's, and no darkness or cloud, magical or not, can block his sight, so for practical purposes he cannot be surprised except by some extraordinary means. Once a day he can summon three demodands of the same type; the summoning takes three segments, and they arrive 1d8 segments later and serve willingly.

His most common avatar is struck only by weapons of +2 or better and has the abilities of a 17th level thief.

Nerull usually carries one or more cursed magic items. Favorites are a necklace of strangulation, a bag of devouring, a rug of smothering and a poisonous cloak. Sometimes he simply leaves them lying where they can hurt the greedy or careless, but usually he uses them as weapons, preferably from behind.

The Life Cutter is really a scythe: at his command a huge blade of red force grows from its tip, counting as a +5 weapon. With it he sweeps an arc of 180 degrees, 10 feet long and 2 feet deep, attacking every creature in it (normal hit roll needed), even those in astral, ethereal or gaseous form. A victim struck must save vs. death or die at once; one who saves takes 5d6 damage. Creatures from, or drawing energy from, the Positive Material Plane take double damage. Undead struck crumble to dust unless they too save vs. death. A successful magic resistance roll cancels the double damage and the death effects, but not the base damage.

Clerics of Nerull

AL any evil; RA rust-red or black garments; AEx 5%; WPN staff*, plus specials; SPH Astral, Combat, Divination (minor), Healing, Guardian, Necromantic, Sun (reversed); SPL none; ADD ebony tendrils, command, pass without trace, sanctuary, hold person, obscurement, withdraw, dispel magic, meld into stone, quest, part water, aerial servant, word of recall, succor

Clerics of Nerull dress in rust-red or black and all carry the skull and scythe, openly or cleverly hidden. They are trained to be alert and are surprised only on a 1. At 1st level they learn to use small sickles (equal to daggers) and at 5th level scythe-like polearms (treat as hook fauchards), in addition to their normal weapons. They never share secrets or confide in anyone.

Ebony Tendrils

This spell summons a lump of blackness five feet across with four 10-foot arms reaching out from it at right angles. Touching the central lump causes death unless a save vs. death is made. The arms attack with the casting cleric's chance to hit, doing d10+2 points of corrosion and crushing damage. A creature struck gets one chance to break free, equal to its chance to open doors. If that is unknown, assume creatures smaller than man-sized escape on 1 on 1d6, man-sized on 1-2, and larger on 1-3.

The round after an arm hits, it pulls back into the central lump, and the victim in its grip must save vs. death. After that the victim is held fast and keeps taking corrosion and crushing damage, but further contact with the lump calls for no more saves vs. death. Broken arms pull back into the lump without attacking again. Arms holding dead creatures keep holding them until the spell ends.

The material components are Nerull's unholy symbol (the skull and scythe) and a small, rusty iron ball.

See the spell compendium for the spell's full statistics.

Pholtus appears as a tall, slender man with a pale face, flowing white hair and bright blue eyes lit with the fire of devotion. He always wears a silky white gown and a cassock trimmed in gold and silver and embroidered with suns and moons. His most common avatar is hit only by weapons of +2 or better.

Once a day Pholtus can summon 1d4 monadic devas. Summoning takes one segment, and after that one deva arrives every two segments.

He carries the Staff of the Silvery Sun, an ivory staff covered in silver and topped with an electrum disc. It acts as a helm of brilliance and a rod of rulership, strikes as a +6 weapon for 1d10+2 damage plus the wielder's strength bonus, and has all the powers of a wand of illumination. It also has these powers:

  • Spectrum beam (four times a day): a beam eight feet wide and 80 feet long. Creatures struck must save vs. spells or fix their eyes on the Staff and obey every command the wielder speaks for 1d6 turns.
  • Brilliant globe (once a day): a globe of 60-foot radius. Everyone in it except Pholtus must save vs. spells or be blinded permanently. Only the Staff, a wish, or a deity able to cure blindness or grant a wish can cure it.

Besides the Staff, Pholtus has the following powers, each usable four times a day, cast at 20th level with a casting time of one segment. Each can also be granted to clerics as a spell, as noted.

  • Dispel darkness: by touching an area of magical darkness, Pholtus makes it vanish; it may form again after eight turns if its duration allows. As a cleric spell, the caster must hold Pholtus' holy symbol and speak a four-segment prayer to him while touching the darkness.
  • Glow: by pointing, Pholtus makes any creature within 80 feet glow as with continual light, but with a 100-foot radius, for eight rounds. There is no saving throw, but magic resistance applies. The light can also shine from Pholtus' face (+2 charisma) or eyes (twin beams 400 feet long and 40 feet wide). As a cleric spell, the caster needs a holy symbol; casting time is five segments and duration one round per level.
  • Reflect: with a mystic gesture and words, Pholtus makes his body reflect all forms of radiation. Creatures using infravision or ultravision who look at him are blinded for 1d8 rounds (save vs. spells negates). In very bright light even creatures with normal sight can be blinded for 2d8 rounds (save vs. spells negates). As a cleric spell, the caster needs a holy symbol and a set of crystal prayer beads; casting time is six segments and duration one round.

Ralishaz usually appears as an ancient, oddly dressed beggar, sometimes male and sometimes female, who begs or gambles. At other times the god appears as a jester or a fool, and at still others as something like his (or her) true form, which is dreadful to see: one moment the face and body are handsome, the next wrinkled and hideous. Through all these changes, scabby beggar or lovely maid, a feeling of unease hangs about the god, for Ralishaz's randomness can be felt and is disturbing. His weapon is always wooden, a staff or a club.

His avatar is hit only by magic weapons, but in keeping with his random nature the plus needed changes from day to day: roll 1d4 for the plus required.

Ralishaz can sometimes turn attacks around. Roll 1d20 for each attack: on 1 it affects both Ralishaz and the attacker; on 2-19 it affects Ralishaz; on 20 it affects the attacker.

The avatar has these powers, each usable once a day at 18th level, with instant casting. Saving throws do not apply, but magic resistance does.

  • Gaze: causes sleep (as the spell) for 1d20 rounds, one creature per round, range 10 feet. Any creature can be affected.
  • Curse: as the spell, with one of these effects: (1) always loses at games of chance; (2) misses his or her next chance at luck (a saving throw or the like); (3) two abilities with different scores swap values; (4) always surprised in the next 1d20 encounters.

Ralishaz always carries the same weapon, though its look changes. It counts as a +3 weapon and does 1-20 damage plus the wielder's strength bonus.

Ulaa can appear as male or female, dwarf, gnome, human or any other creature she likes, but all her guises tend to have dwarflike proportions and a gnomish face. She usually wears adamantite chain mail with a gem-studded harness, and always carries a magic military pick and a hammer of thunderbolts.

Ulaa is immune to all earth-based spells and can pass through earth or rock at 18" per turn. Creatures of the Elemental Plane of Earth respect her: good or neutral ones serve faithfully when she asks, and evil ones flee at the sight of her. Her hearing is twice as keen as a human's, and she has infravision to 240 feet and ultravision.

Her most common avatar is hit only by weapons of +3 or better and regenerates one hit point per round while touching earth or stone. In any form she can cast these spells, one at a time, once per round, at 12th level:

  • Once a day: earthquake, statue, move earth, glassteel, wall of stone, conjure earth elemental (24 HD).
  • Twice a day: transmute rock to mud, stone to flesh, flesh to stone, wall of stone.
  • Three times a day: passwall, dimension door, stone shape, glassee, wall of force.

Wall of stone is printed in both the once-a-day and twice-a-day lists.

Her military pick is +5. She can throw the hammer of thunderbolts every other round to a range of 140 feet without needing rest. Her most common avatar does 2d4+12 damage to large opponents with it (if it does not kill them outright; see the DMG). Against small opponents (under 1 hit die) she can slay 2d4+12 hit dice of creatures with each hammer attack.
